name: Bagchen
description: Bagchen (meaning 'Great Game' or 'Bird Game') is the national domino game of Tibet. Played with a double set of Chinese dominoes (64 tiles), it is a sophisticated trick-taking game similar to the Chinese classic Tien Gow. However, Bagchen introduces a brutal 'Scorched Earth' victory condition: winning individual tricks is merely a means to an end; the only trick that truly matters is the very last one. It involves complex 'set' leading, where players can play up to four tiles at once in coordinated formations.

content.text: Bagchen (meaning 'Great Game' or 'Bird Game') is the national domino game of Tibet. Played with a double set of Chinese dominoes (64 tiles), it is a sophisticated trick-taking game similar to the Chinese classic Tien Gow. However, Bagchen introduces a brutal 'Scorched Earth' victory condition: winning individual tricks is merely a means to an end; the only trick that truly matters is the very last one. It involves complex 'set' leading, where players can play up to four tiles at once in coordinated formations.

Rooted in the ancient trade routes between Tibet and China. While it shares the civil/military tile hierarchy with Chinese Tien Gow, Bagchen evolved in the monasteries and aristocrat circles of Lhasa into a distinct game with unique scoring and grouping rules.
4 players. No partnerships; play is clockwise.
Two sets of Chinese dominoes (32 x 2 = 64). Each tile represents two dice faces.
64 tiles, traditionally stored in a carved wooden box. A bowl for tokens/chips.
Each player receives 16 tiles. Tiles are usually arranged in 'stacks' or 'walls' before being drawn.

items.text: Lhasa Short Game: A version where only 12 tricks are played (8 tiles per player) for faster sessions.
